source.title: The Rogue Scalpel: Activation Steering Compromises LLM Safety
source.authors: Anton Korznikov; Andrey V. Galichin; Alexey Dontsov; Oleg Y. Rogov; I. Oseledets; Elena Tutubalina

record.tranche_reason: Tests harmful compliance under activation steering, a different inference-time intervention from the fine-tuning and response-token mechanisms in the claim.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own harmful-compliance results for activation steering. It does not test fine-tuning, prefilling, suffixes, decoding changes, per-token KL, safety localization in weights or ranks, or deepening safety training. Fine-tuning and token-depth studies are cited only. The judge-precision validation and the cited fine-tuning results are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study measures harmful compliance under inference-time activation steering, using random and SAE directions added to the residual stream. None of the claim's versions names that intervention. There is no harmful or benign fine-tuning (V1, V2), no per-token KL (V3), and no prefill, suffix or decoding change (V4). Steering acts on activations, not on a small set of weights or ranks (V5). Nothing on the cause of shallowness (V6) or on deepening training (V7). Qi et al. (2310.03693) is cited in related work only. The reader's 'tests/T3' is therefore corrected: the results are a related construct and belong under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also stress three further points. Benign SAE features are about as harmful as random directions (1–4% higher). Feature effects generalize poorly across prompts, which makes safety screening impractical. The universal vector's benefit is model-dependent.
record.recipe_differences: Uses inference-time residual-stream activation addition rather than fine-tuning or token-position KL measurement; it does not test whether safety is concentrated in response-opening tokens.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported outcomes vary with model, steering coefficient, intervention layer, and vector type. Random steering is described as most effective in middle or early layers; excessive coefficients can reduce coherence. Prompt/category susceptibility and cross-prompt generalization also vary.

fits_no_version.finding: Random and benign SAE activation-steering directions raise harmful compliance from 0% to about 1–18%, depending on model, layer, coefficient and prompt.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Inference-time activation steering, even with random or benign directions, can break refusal in instruct-tuned models.

fits_no_version.finding: Many SAE features jailbreak some prompt (817/1000), but generalize poorly across prompts; the best feature breaks 35 of 100.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Steering-induced jailbreaks are widespread but prompt-specific.

fits_no_version.finding: The most harmful SAE features have near-zero cosine similarity to the refusal direction.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Steering jailbreaks do not work through linear alignment with the refusal direction.

fits_no_version.finding: A benign 'brand identity' feature, applied via the Goodfire API, yields 'disclaimer-then-compliance' and fictional-framing responses.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Public steering APIs with benign features can elicit harmful compliance (qualitative).

fits_no_version.finding: Averaging 20 random vectors selected on one prompt raises compliance on unseen prompts about 4x on average. The effect is model-dependent and lower for Qwen2.5-32B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Prompt-specific steering vulnerabilities aggregate into a more universal attack.

record.problems: Compliance-rate uncertainty estimates are not stated. The Goodfire API examples are qualitative and do not report a rate. SAE-feature counts for features jailbreaking at least five prompts conflict: the body says 353, while the Fig. 5 caption says 668/1000. The judge validation is a selected sample of 100 responses classified harmful by the judge, rather than an overall accuracy estimate.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the 60-row limit. MMLU capability scores are not included because they measure general capability costs rather than harmful compliance. The report of poor cross-category generalization is noted in fits_no_version but has no numerical value in the text.

untested.parts: No aligned-vs-base per-token KL or position analysis.
No prefilling, adversarial suffix or decoding change. Activation steering is a different intervention.
No weight or rank localization. The cosine test against the refusal direction (R17) concerns activations, not parameters.
No test of data or objective as the cause of shallowness.

record.verdict_notes: The 'disclaimer-then-compliance' pattern in R18–R22 is loosely reminiscent of shallow alignment: an opening refusal-like disclaimer is followed by compliance. However, the paper measures no token positions and does not frame it this way, so no version link is made. Appendix C gives counts of random vectors jailbreaking at least five prompts (Llama 387, Qwen 313). These are not rows, but they bear on no version. MMLU capability results are correctly left out.

versions.untested_parts: No harmful fine-tuning or fine-tuning data-size sweep.
No compliant-opening prefill, adversarial suffix, or decoding-change test; steering is not used to test whether bypassing the opening tokens defeats safety.
No test of whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behaviour.
No test of whether training data or objective causes safety to be shallow.
No training to deepen safety across response tokens, or evaluation of whether such training holds up.
